subject: ela
intro: Each problem includes the full informational passage it depends on. These passages are longer and may cover more than one subtopic, include numbers or technical words, or shift from a problem to a solution. Read carefully across the whole passage. The central idea is the main point the author develops about the topic, not a one-word topic and not a single supporting detail. An objective summary states that central idea and the key supporting points in order, leaving out personal opinions, judgments, and reactions. Watch for distractors that capture only one section, that quietly insert an opinion, or that overweight a single fact.

items.prompt:
Read the passage, then answer.

For most of human history, people lit their homes with fire. They burned candles made of animal fat, then whale oil lamps, then gas jets that hissed in the walls. Each new method gave more light, but each also brought danger. Open flames started fires, filled rooms with smoke, and had to be tended constantly. When Thomas Edison and others perfected the electric light bulb in the late 1800s, the change was not simply brighter rooms. Electric light could be switched on with the touch of a finger, it produced no flame, and it did not foul the air. Factories that had closed at sunset could now run through the night, and workers no longer had to strain their eyes by dim lamplight. Cities installed electric streetlights, and neighborhoods that had emptied after dark filled with people. Reading, sewing, and studying after sunset stopped being luxuries reserved for the wealthy, who alone could afford steady oil. The bulb itself was a small thing, but it rearranged how people used their hours. The day no longer ended when the sun went down. In time, the wiring strung up to carry electricity to lamps would also carry it to motors, refrigerators, and machines no one had yet imagined. The humble light bulb, in other words, was the doorway through which electricity entered ordinary life.

Which statement best expresses the central idea of the whole passage, and which detail most directly develops it?
items.answer: Central idea: The electric light bulb did far more than brighten rooms; it changed how people lived and worked and opened the way for electricity to enter everyday life. The detail that most directly develops it is that factories could run through the night and reading or studying after dark stopped being a luxury, showing the bulb reshaped people's hours, not just their lighting.

steps: Read across the whole passage, not just the opening history of candles and oil lamps.
Notice the author moves from 'brighter rooms' to larger effects: night work, safer air, streetlights, and finally electricity powering motors and machines.
State the central idea as the main point developed across the text: the bulb transformed daily life and ushered in the age of electricity, not merely 'the bulb made light.'
Reject 'the history of lighting' as a topic, not a central idea, and reject 'electric light has no flame' as a single supporting detail.
Choose the detail about factories running at night and reading no longer being a luxury, because it directly shows the bulb changed how people used their time.

Read the passage, then answer.

Honeybees are famous for making honey, but their most important work has nothing to do with the jars on a grocery shelf. As a bee moves from flower to flower gathering nectar, grains of pollen stick to the tiny hairs on its body. When the bee visits the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off, fertilizing the plant so it can produce fruit and seeds. This process, called pollination, is how a huge share of the world's food crops reproduce. Apples, almonds, blueberries, cucumbers, and melons all depend on insect pollinators, and honeybees do much of that work. Scientists estimate that about one out of every three bites of food a person eats exists because of pollinators. Yet in recent years beekeepers have reported losing large numbers of their hives. Several causes seem to be at work at once: certain pesticides, a parasitic mite that weakens bees, the spread of disease, and the loss of wildflower meadows where bees feed. No single villain explains the decline, which is part of what makes it so hard to stop. Researchers are testing safer pesticides, breeding bees that resist mites, and encouraging farmers and even city dwellers to plant flowers bees can use. The story of the honeybee is a reminder that a small, easily overlooked creature can hold up an enormous part of the system that feeds us, and that protecting it may require many solutions working together.

Which statement best expresses the central idea of the whole passage?
items.answer: Central idea: Honeybees matter far more for the pollination that supports much of our food supply than for honey, and because their decline has several causes at once, protecting them will require many solutions working together. This captures both subtopics, the bees' importance and the layered threat to them.

steps: Identify the topic, honeybees, then look for the main point the author builds about it.
The first part argues bees matter for pollination, not honey, supported by the 'one in three bites' statistic and the list of crops.
The second part explains the decline has multiple causes and therefore needs multiple solutions.
A central idea that names only pollination, or only the decline, captures one section but not the whole passage.
The full central idea ties the two halves together: bees are vital, and saving them takes many combined efforts.

Read the passage, then read the three summaries and answer.

The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is often pictured as a solid island of trash floating in the ocean, but that image is wrong. It is actually a vast region where currents gather floating plastic, and most of that plastic has broken into tiny pieces called microplastics, spread thinly through the water like pepper stirred into soup. Because the pieces are small and scattered, the patch cannot be seen from a passing ship or even clearly from space. This makes it far harder to clean up than a floating island would be. Sea animals mistake the small fragments for food. The plastic does not simply vanish; sunlight and waves only grind it into ever smaller bits, which can remain in the ocean for centuries. Some engineers have built floating systems to skim plastic from the surface, and these can collect large debris, but they cannot capture the tiniest particles or the plastic that has already sunk. For that reason, many scientists argue that the most effective response is to stop plastic from reaching the ocean in the first place, by reducing single-use plastic and improving waste collection on land.

Which of the following is the most accurate and objective summary of the passage?
1) The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is the most disgusting and shameful thing humans have ever done, and everyone must stop using plastic today.
2) The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is not a solid island but a wide area of mostly tiny, scattered microplastics that are hard to see and clean up. Skimming systems help with large debris but miss the smallest pieces, so many scientists say the best response is to keep plastic from reaching the ocean.
3) The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is full of plastic, and skimming machines float on the surface to scoop up the larger pieces of trash.
items.answer: Summary 2. It accurately states the central idea, that the patch is scattered microplastics rather than an island and is therefore hard to clean, and includes the key points about skimmers' limits and prevention on land, all without inserting opinions.

steps: An objective summary states the central idea and key points in order and contains no opinions.
Summary 1 buries the central idea under the judgments 'disgusting,' 'shameful,' and the command 'must stop using plastic today,' so it is opinionated.
Summary 3 reports only one detail, the skimming machines, and omits the central idea that the patch is scattered microplastics and that prevention matters, so it is incomplete.
Summary 2 captures the main point and the supporting points in logical order with no opinion words, so it is the accurate, objective summary.

Read the passage, then answer.

When people think of deserts, they picture endless sand and lifeless heat, but the Sonoran Desert of the American Southwest tells a different story. It is one of the wettest deserts on Earth, soaked twice a year by gentle winter rains and powerful summer storms. This unusual rhythm of water supports a surprising web of life. The towering saguaro cactus, which can live for two hundred years and grow taller than a house, stores rainwater in its pleated trunk, swelling after a storm and shrinking slowly through the dry months. Its white flowers open at night to be pollinated by bats, and its red fruit feeds birds, coyotes, and people. Holes that woodpeckers carve into the saguaro become nests for tiny elf owls. Beneath the ground, many small animals escape the daytime heat in burrows, emerging at dusk to hunt. Even the desert's plants cooperate; young saguaros often sprout in the shade of a 'nurse tree' such as a palo verde, which shelters the seedling until it is strong enough to stand on its own. Far from being empty, the Sonoran Desert is a tightly connected community in which water, plants, and animals depend on one another to survive a climate that only looks barren.

Which statement best expresses the central idea, and name one detail that develops it.
items.answer: Central idea: The Sonoran Desert is not the empty wasteland people imagine but a wet, tightly connected community in which water, plants, and animals depend on one another to survive. A developing detail is that the saguaro stores rainwater and provides flowers, fruit, and woodpecker holes that feed and shelter bats, birds, coyotes, and elf owls, showing how the life of the desert is interconnected.

steps: The author opens by overturning the stereotype of an empty, lifeless desert, signaling the real point will be the opposite.
Details across the passage, the twice-yearly rain, the saguaro's many uses, the nurse tree, build the idea of an interdependent community.
State the central idea as that full point, not the topic 'the desert' and not a single fact like 'saguaros can live two hundred years.'
Pick a detail that shows interdependence, such as the saguaro feeding and sheltering many animals, or the palo verde nursing young cacti.
Connect the chosen detail to the main point: it demonstrates that life in the desert is linked, not isolated.

Before the 1700s, doctors had no reliable way to prevent smallpox, a disease that killed or scarred millions. In some parts of the world, people noticed that survivors of smallpox never caught it again, and they tried a risky practice of deliberately giving healthy people a mild case. In England, a country doctor named Edward Jenner heard a piece of folk wisdom: milkmaids who had caught cowpox, a far milder illness, seemed protected from smallpox. In 1796 Jenner tested the idea. He took fluid from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid's hand and scratched it into the arm of a young boy. The boy fell mildly ill, then recovered. Weeks later Jenner exposed him to smallpox, and the boy did not get sick. By using a harmless disease to train the body's defenses against a deadly one, Jenner had created the first vaccine. At first many people distrusted the idea of putting material from a cow into a human body. Over time, though, the evidence won out, and vaccination spread across the world. The principle Jenner demonstrated, that the body can be taught to fight a disease it has not yet met, became the foundation of modern immunization. In 1980, after a worldwide vaccination campaign, smallpox became the first human disease ever completely wiped out.

Which statement best expresses the central idea of the whole passage?
items.answer: Central idea: By testing the folk observation that cowpox protected against smallpox, Edward Jenner created the first vaccine and established the principle, the foundation of modern immunization, that the body can be taught to fight a disease before it meets it. This captures the discovery and its lasting importance, not just one event.

steps: Trace the passage from the danger of smallpox, to Jenner's experiment, to the lasting principle and the eradication of the disease.
The main point is not merely 'Jenner scratched cowpox into a boy'; that single event is a supporting detail.
The author stresses that Jenner's work became 'the foundation of modern immunization,' signaling the broader central idea.
Reject a too-narrow choice that covers only the experiment and a topic choice like 'smallpox.'
The full central idea links the discovery to its principle and lasting impact on medicine.

Maps seem to tell the simple truth about where places are, but every flat map of the round Earth contains a hidden distortion. The problem is geometric: you cannot peel the curved surface of a globe and lay it flat without stretching or tearing it somewhere, just as you cannot flatten an orange peel without ripping it. Mapmakers solve this with projections, mathematical methods of spreading the globe onto a flat sheet, and every projection sacrifices accuracy in something to preserve accuracy in something else. The familiar Mercator projection, useful for navigation because it keeps directions true, badly exaggerates the size of land near the poles. On a Mercator map, Greenland looks as large as Africa, though Africa is in fact about fourteen times bigger. Other projections keep sizes honest but bend the shapes of continents. Because no flat map can be perfectly faithful in every way, the 'right' map depends on what you need it for, and a careful reader learns to ask what a given map distorts.

Which statement best expresses the central idea?
1) Greenland looks as big as Africa on a Mercator map.
2) Every flat map of the round Earth must distort something, so no projection is perfectly accurate, and the best map depends on its purpose.
3) Maps.
items.answer: Statement 2. It states the main point the author develops across the passage, that flattening a round Earth forces every map to distort something and no single map is perfectly accurate. Statement 1 is one supporting detail and statement 3 is only a topic.

steps: The central idea is the main point built across the whole passage, not a single fact or a one-word topic.
Statement 3, 'Maps,' is only the topic, not a complete idea.
Statement 1 is a single supporting detail, the Greenland example, used to illustrate the larger point.
Statement 2 captures the point the orange-peel comparison, the projections, and the Mercator example all build toward.
Therefore statement 2 is the central idea.

Read the passage, then answer.

For decades, a steady stream of cargo ships, fishing boats, and ferries crossed the harbor, and the gray whales that migrate along the coast had to share the water with engine noise. Whales rely on sound to find food, stay together, and sense their surroundings, and the constant rumble of propellers can drown out the calls they depend on. Then, for a short time, ship traffic in the bay fell sharply when a regional shipping route was rerouted during repairs to the main channel. Scientists who had placed underwater microphones in the bay noticed something unexpected. With fewer ships, the level of background noise dropped, and the whales began calling to one another more often and at a lower, calmer pitch. Stress chemicals measured in the water around the animals declined as well. When the channel reopened and the ships returned, the noise climbed back and the whales' behavior shifted again toward the strained, louder calls. The episode gave researchers a rare natural experiment. It suggested that ocean noise is not just an annoyance to whales but a genuine source of stress that shapes how they communicate, and it raised a practical question of whether quieter ships or rerouted lanes could ease that burden.

Which statement best expresses the central idea, and which detail most directly develops it?
items.answer: Central idea: Ship noise is a real source of stress for whales that interferes with how they communicate, and the temporary drop in traffic acted as a natural experiment showing that reducing noise could help them. The detail that most directly develops it is that when ships left, the whales called more often at a calmer pitch and their stress chemicals fell, then reversed when ships returned.

steps: Identify what the author argues across the passage: ocean noise harms whales, and the quiet period offered evidence.
The before-and-after change in the whales' calls and stress chemicals is the core evidence, so it is the developing detail.
State the central idea as a full point, not the topic 'whales and ships' and not the lone fact 'the route was rerouted for repairs.'
Reject a too-narrow idea that mentions only that whales use sound, since the passage builds toward noise as a stressor.
Connect the chosen detail to the main point: the matched change in noise and behavior is what shows the noise truly affects the whales.

Read the passage, then read the draft summary and answer.

The printing press, built by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440, did not invent the book, but it changed who could own one. Before the press, every book in Europe was copied by hand, usually by monks, a process so slow that a single Bible could take a scribe more than a year. Books were therefore rare and costly, owned mostly by churches, universities, and the wealthy. Gutenberg's machine used movable metal letters that could be arranged, inked, and pressed onto paper, then rearranged for the next page. A print shop could produce hundreds of identical copies in the time it once took to hand-copy one. Prices fell, and books began to reach merchants, students, and eventually ordinary households. As reading material spread, so did literacy, new ideas, and arguments that authorities could no longer easily contain. The press helped power the scientific revolution and the religious upheavals of the following centuries.

A student wrote this summary:
'Gutenberg built the printing press around 1440. Before it, books were copied slowly by hand and were rare and expensive. The press could make many identical copies cheaply, so books spread to ordinary people, which boosted literacy and the spread of new ideas. Honestly, this was the greatest invention in all of history and everyone should be grateful for it.'

Which sentence in the summary should be removed to keep it objective, and why?
items.answer: The last sentence, 'Honestly, this was the greatest invention in all of history and everyone should be grateful for it,' should be removed. It is a personal opinion and judgment, not a statement of what the passage actually says, so it makes the summary no longer objective.

steps: An objective summary reports only what the text states and leaves out the writer's reactions and judgments.
Check each sentence: the first four report facts from the passage, the date, the slow hand-copying, the cheap copies, and the spread of literacy and ideas.
The final sentence calls it 'the greatest invention in all of history' and says people 'should be grateful,' which are the student's opinions.
Those claims are not in the passage and express a judgment, so they break objectivity.
Removing that sentence leaves an accurate, opinion-free summary of the central idea and key points.

Read the passage, then answer.

At first glance, a coral reef looks like colorful rock, but it is built and kept alive by tiny animals called coral polyps, each no bigger than a grain of rice. The polyps pull minerals from seawater to build hard limestone cups around themselves, and over thousands of years these cups pile into the vast structures we call reefs. The polyps themselves are not green or gold; their color comes from microscopic algae that live inside their bodies. The two partners help each other. The algae use sunlight to make food and share it with the coral, and in return the coral gives the algae a protected home. This partnership works only within a narrow range of warm temperatures. When the water grows too hot, the coral expels the algae, loses both its color and its main food source, and turns ghostly white, an event called bleaching. A bleached coral is not yet dead, and if cool water returns soon enough the algae can come back. But if the heat lasts, the coral starves. As ocean temperatures rise, bleaching events have grown more frequent and severe, threatening reefs that shelter a quarter of all ocean species. Understanding that a reef is a living partnership, not a lifeless rock, helps explain both why it is so productive and why it is so fragile.

Which statement best expresses the central idea of the whole passage?
items.answer: Central idea: A coral reef is not lifeless rock but a living partnership between coral polyps and algae, and because that partnership depends on a narrow temperature range, rising ocean heat makes reefs both remarkably productive and dangerously fragile. This ties the partnership to the threat, covering the whole passage.

steps: Notice the passage has two linked parts: how the reef is a coral-algae partnership, and why warming makes it fragile through bleaching.
A central idea naming only the partnership, or only bleaching, captures one section, not the whole text.
Reject the topic 'coral reefs' and the single detail 'polyps are the size of a grain of rice.'
The closing sentence signals the unifying point: the partnership explains both the reef's productivity and its fragility.
The best central idea joins the partnership and its temperature-driven vulnerability.

For years, the small town of Brightwater struggled with flooding. Every heavy rain sent water pouring off its paved streets and rooftops faster than the storm drains could carry it, and basements filled while the nearby creek overflowed. The town council first proposed building larger concrete drains, but the cost was enormous and engineers warned that bigger pipes would simply rush even more water into the creek downstream. Instead, the town tried a different approach known as green infrastructure. Workers tore up some pavement and replaced it with gardens of deep-rooted plants that soak up rain. They built shallow basins in parks to hold water and let it sink slowly into the ground, and they planted trees whose roots and leaves capture rainfall. Rather than racing storm water away, these methods slow it down and let the land absorb it. Within three years, flooding in the worst neighborhoods had dropped sharply, the gardens drew birds and insects back to the town, and the project had cost less than the giant pipes would have. Brightwater's experience showed that working with nature, rather than only against water, could solve a problem that concrete alone could not.

Which of the following is the most accurate and objective summary?
1) Brightwater faced repeated flooding. Instead of building costly larger drains that would worsen downstream flooding, the town used green infrastructure such as rain gardens, basins, and trees to absorb storm water. Within three years flooding dropped, wildlife returned, and the project cost less than the pipes.
2) Brightwater used to flood, but its leaders were finally smart enough to plant some gardens, which proves every town should abandon concrete forever.
3) Brightwater planted deep-rooted gardens and trees that drew birds and insects back to the town.
items.answer: Summary 1. It states the central idea, that Brightwater solved its flooding by choosing green infrastructure over larger drains, and lists the key supporting points in order without any opinions.

steps: An objective summary captures the central idea and key points in order, free of opinion.
Summary 2 inserts the judgments 'finally smart enough' and the overstated claim that every town 'should abandon concrete forever,' so it is opinionated.
Summary 3 reports only the wildlife detail and omits the flooding problem, the rejected drain plan, and the drop in flooding, so it is incomplete.
Summary 1 includes the problem, the rejected option, the green solution, and the results in logical order with no opinion words, so it is the best summary.

Read the passage, then answer.

The word 'tornado' brings to mind a single dark funnel, but the storms that breed tornadoes follow a pattern scientists have learned to read. Most violent tornadoes are born from supercells, towering thunderstorms in which the rising air begins to spin. The spin starts high in the storm, where winds at different heights blow in different directions and speeds, a condition called wind shear that sets the air rolling like a pencil between two hands. As warm, moist air surges upward into the storm, it tilts that rolling air upright and stretches it into a tall, rotating column. If this rotation tightens and reaches the ground, a tornado forms. Because the ingredients, warm moist air below, cool dry air above, and strong wind shear, often come together over the central United States in spring, that region earns the nickname Tornado Alley. Forecasters cannot yet say exactly where a single tornado will touch down, but by watching for these ingredients on radar and weather balloons, they can warn that conditions are ripe, sometimes giving people precious minutes to take shelter. The funnel that frightens us, in other words, is the final visible step in a chain of invisible conditions that scientists are steadily learning to anticipate.

Which statement best expresses the central idea, and which detail most directly develops it?
items.answer: Central idea: A tornado is the final visible result of a chain of conditions, warm moist air, cool dry air, and wind shear inside supercell storms, that scientists have learned to read in order to warn people in advance. The detail that most directly develops it is the explanation that wind shear sets the air spinning and rising warm air stretches it into a rotating column that can reach the ground.

steps: The author moves from the familiar funnel to the hidden conditions that produce it, ending by calling the funnel 'the final visible step.'
State the central idea as that full point: tornadoes arise from a readable chain of conditions forecasters can detect.
Reject the topic 'tornadoes' and the lone fact 'the central U.S. is called Tornado Alley.'
The detail explaining how wind shear and rising warm air create the rotating column directly develops the idea that the funnel is the end of a chain.
Connect that detail to the main point: it shows the invisible conditions that lead to the visible storm.

We tend to call the dictionary the authority on what words 'really' mean, as if it set the rules and we obeyed them. The truth runs the other way. Lexicographers, the people who write dictionaries, do not invent definitions or decide which words are allowed. They are more like reporters than judges. They read enormous collections of writing and speech, watching how people actually use words, and they record those uses. When a new word like 'selfie' spreads widely enough, or an old word takes on a new sense, the editors add it, because their job is to describe the living language, not to freeze it. This is why dictionaries change with every edition and why a word's meaning can drift over the years. A dictionary, then, is a snapshot of how a community is using its language at a moment in time, not a law book handed down from above. Knowing this changes how we read it: a definition tells us how people use a word, which is something we can always observe and test, rather than a permanent rule we must simply accept.

Which statement best expresses the central idea?
1) The word 'selfie' was added to dictionaries after it became popular.
2) Dictionaries describe how people actually use language and change over time, rather than setting fixed, permanent rules for what words must mean.
3) Lexicographers.
items.answer: Statement 2. It expresses the main point the author develops, that dictionaries describe living usage and change over time instead of dictating permanent rules. Statement 1 is one supporting example and statement 3 is only a topic.

steps: Look for the point built across the whole passage, signaled by the contrast between a 'law book' and a 'snapshot.'
Statement 3 names only a topic, the people who write dictionaries, not a full idea.
Statement 1 is a single example, 'selfie,' used to support the larger claim.
Statement 2 states the central idea: dictionaries record real usage and change, rather than fixing meaning.
Therefore statement 2 is the central idea.

Read the passage, then answer.

Nothing seems more permanent than a mountain, yet mountains are temporary, locked in a slow contest between forces that build them up and forces that wear them down. Mountains rise where the giant plates of the Earth's crust collide and crumple, pushing rock upward over millions of years. The Himalayas, the tallest range on Earth, are still growing today as the plate carrying India pushes into Asia. But the moment rock is lifted into the air, it comes under attack. Rain, ice, and wind chip at the peaks; rivers carve valleys and carry away the loosened sediment grain by grain. Freezing water widens cracks until slabs break free in landslides. These forces of erosion never rest. A young, growing range like the Himalayas has jagged, towering peaks because uplift is winning the race. An old range like the Appalachians, once as tall as the Himalayas, now has low, rounded ridges because erosion has had hundreds of millions of years to wear it down while uplift has stopped. Whether a mountain is rising or shrinking depends on which side of this contest is ahead. To read a mountain's shape, then, is to read the score in a battle between the building force from below and the wearing force from above.

Which statement best expresses the central idea, and name one detail that develops it.
items.answer: Central idea: Mountains are not permanent but are shaped by an ongoing contest between uplift that builds them and erosion that wears them down, so a mountain's shape reveals which force is winning. A developing detail is the contrast between the jagged, growing Himalayas, where uplift is winning, and the low, rounded Appalachians, where erosion has worn down a once-tall range.

steps: The author frames the whole passage as a 'contest' or 'battle' between building up and wearing down.
State the central idea as that full point: mountains change over time according to which force, uplift or erosion, is ahead.
Reject the topic 'mountains' and the single fact 'the Himalayas are the tallest range.'
Choose a detail that shows the contest, such as the Himalayas-versus-Appalachians comparison or rivers carrying away sediment.
Connect the detail to the main point: the comparison shows the same forces produce different shapes depending on which is winning.

The Transcontinental Railroad, completed in 1869, connected the eastern United States to the Pacific coast for the first time by rail. Before it, crossing the continent meant months of dangerous travel by wagon or a long sea voyage around South America. The railroad cut that journey to about a week. Two companies built toward each other, one laying track eastward from California through the steep Sierra Nevada mountains, the other westward from Nebraska across the plains. Much of the most brutal labor, blasting tunnels through solid granite and laying track in deep snow, was done by thousands of Chinese and Irish immigrant workers, many of whom were injured or killed. The finished line transformed the country. Goods, mail, and people moved across the continent at a speed never before possible, towns sprang up along the route, and national markets grew. At the same time, the railroad pushed deeper into the lands of Native American nations, disrupting their ways of life and the herds of bison they depended on.

A student wrote this summary:
'The Transcontinental Railroad, finished in 1869, linked the eastern United States to the Pacific by rail and cut a months-long journey to about a week. Two companies built toward each other, relying heavily on Chinese and Irish immigrant labor under dangerous conditions. The railroad sped up travel and trade and helped towns grow, but it also pushed into Native American lands and disrupted their way of life. The brave workers were the real heroes and should be celebrated above everyone else.'

Which sentence should be removed to keep the summary objective, and why?
items.answer: The last sentence, 'The brave workers were the real heroes and should be celebrated above everyone else,' should be removed. Calling the workers 'heroes' who 'should be celebrated' is a personal opinion and judgment, not a statement of what the passage says, so it makes the summary no longer objective.

steps: An objective summary reports only the text's information and excludes the writer's opinions.
The first three sentences accurately restate the railroad's effect on travel, the immigrant labor, and the costs to Native nations.
The final sentence praises the workers as 'heroes' who 'should be celebrated above everyone else,' which is a judgment.
That praise is the student's reaction, not a fact stated in the passage, so it breaks objectivity.
Removing it leaves an accurate, opinion-free summary of the central idea and key points.

Read the passage, then answer.

Sleep can look like wasted time, hours when the body does nothing, but research shows the opposite is true: the brain is hard at work while we rest. During sleep the brain replays and strengthens the connections formed while we were awake, which helps move new facts and skills from short-term to long-term memory. Students who sleep well after studying remember more than those who stay up cramming. Sleep also acts as a cleaning crew. As we rest, fluid flushes through the brain and clears away waste products that build up during the day, including some linked to disease. Meanwhile the body repairs muscle, balances the chemicals that control hunger and mood, and strengthens the immune system that fights illness. This is why losing sleep does more than make a person tired; it weakens memory, dims attention, sours mood, and lowers the body's defenses. Scientists now treat sleep not as an optional luxury but as a basic biological need, as essential to health as food and water. Far from being idle, the sleeping brain and body are busy doing repairs and housekeeping that can only happen when we step away from the waking world.

Which statement best expresses the central idea, and which detail most directly develops it?
items.answer: Central idea: Sleep is not wasted or idle time but an active, essential process in which the brain and body strengthen memory, clear waste, repair themselves, and defend against illness, making it as necessary to health as food and water. The detail that most directly develops it is that during sleep the brain replays and strengthens connections to store memories and fluid flushes waste from the brain, showing real work is being done.

steps: The passage opens by overturning the idea that sleep is wasted time, signaling the main point is the opposite.
State the central idea as that full point: sleep is active, essential work for the brain and body, not idle time.
Reject the topic 'sleep' and a single fact like 'students who sleep remember more.'
Choose a detail that shows the brain at work, such as strengthening memory connections or flushing waste, since these directly prove sleep is productive.
Connect the detail to the main point: it demonstrates that the resting brain and body are busy with necessary tasks.
